L6.1.quote: Conversely, suppose $x>a_1$ belongs to $S$. Because the sequence is strictly increasing, it is unbounded. Choose the unique $n$ for which $a_n<x\le a_{n+1}$. Since $x\in S$, it has gcd greater than 1 with each of $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. The minimality in the definition of $a_{n+1}$ therefore gives $a_{n+1}\le x$. Hence $x=a_{n+1}$.
L6.1.note: Correct: the sequence is the increasing enumeration of integers >= a_1 non-coprime to all terms; the minimality argument is valid for all cases.

L6.2.quote: If a family of finite sets is pairwise intersecting and has a member $C$ of size $r$, then it has only finitely many inclusion-minimal finite transversals.
L6.2.note: This general lemma is false (e.g. F_k={x_1,...,x_k,y_k} is pairwise intersecting with infinitely many minimal transversals); the tree argument is invalid, and no large-prime erasure is ever given.

L6.3.quote: Take $y=a_n$. Then $a_n+L\in S$, and among the integers strictly greater than $a_n$ and at most $a_n+L$ there are exactly $T$ members of $S$. Since the terms of the sequence are the increasing enumeration of $S$ from $a_1$ onward, the $T$-th term after $a_n$ is therefore $a_n+L$.
L6.3.note: The counting/periodicity assembly is complete and starts at n=1, but membership depending only on residues mod L rests entirely on the false transversal lemma.

parsed.notes: L6.1 is correctly proved. Finiteness rests on a false 'finite-transversal lemma': pairwise-intersecting families of finite sets can have infinitely many minimal transversals (e.g. F_k={x_1,...,x_k,y_k}); the König-tree argument is invalid and no large-prime erasure is given. Periodicity assembly is correct but conditional; wrong_answer_stated: true.
